tweet.text:
Most people are using Claude Code wrong.

They're burning Opus tokens on work Haiku could handle in parallel.

Opus reviews. Sonnet builds. Haiku swarms.

Anthropic's multi-agent workflow lets you split the work:

→ Sonnet runs the main session, writes code, and executes tests
→ Haiku subagents search files, scan code, and fetch docs in parallel
→ Opus reviews architecture, catches regressions, and audits the final diff

the setup starts with one command:

`CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL=haiku claude --model sonnet`

then keep Opus on call at 3 checkpoints:

→ before locking the implementation plan
→ when the same test fails twice
→ before declaring the task done

why waste your best model searching 30 files or reading API docs?

let Haiku do the grunt work. let Sonnet build. bring Opus in when the decisions actually matter.

the real win? isolated subagents keep hundreds of thousands of tokens of search results and logs out of your main context.

want to set this up?
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents
paste the prompt below into Claude Code to configure the agents, delegation rules, and worktree isolation.

https://x.com/mirku21/status/2109026276048769472/video/1

article.title: How I run Claude Code in YOLO mode without getting burned

blocks.text: Most of us run coding agents with auto-approve on now.
Claude Code with --dangerously-skip-permissions, Codex with approvals off, Cursor in YOLO mode.
I do too. Approving dozens of tool calls to fix one test is not a workflow.

But here is the part people skip: an agent that approves its own tool calls has whatever access you have. Your SSH keys. Your browser sessions. Your home folder. Your ~/.aws credentials. Every token sitting in your shell environment.

This is not theoretical. Earlier this month a developer reported that Claude Code deleted 48,218 live files in 103 seconds while working on what was supposed to be an isolated copy of the project. A cleanup script followed Windows folder links into the real one.
That is not a reason to stop. It is a reason to set things up so a bad run costs you nothing.
Anthropic's own docs say it plainly: use bypassPermissions mode only in isolated environments like containers or VMs where Claude Code can't cause damage.
So this is my setup. Five layers. Each one is small, and together they let me leave the agent running without watching it.
Layer 1: Split the models
YOLO mode means more tool calls, more subagents, more tokens. If everything runs on your biggest model, you pay top rates for grep.
The split:
Opus plans
Sonnet writes the code
Haiku handles subagents: file search, codebase exploration, summaries
Haiku 5.5 shipped this week. Anthropic prices it at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens for prompts up to 100K tokens, versus $1 and $5 for Haiku 4.5.
Their estimate is that it costs around 75% less to run than Haiku 4.5 on average, once you account for its new tokenizer. That makes it the obvious pick for background work.
Claude Code has a built-in alias for the first two. opusplan uses Opus in plan mode and switches to Sonnet for execution.
For subagents, set a default model in settings.json:

One catch from the docs: this variable alone does not change the built-in Explore and Plan subagents. To move exploration onto Haiku, define your own Explore in .claude/agents/Explore.md. It overrides the built-in one and keeps its own model:
To check it worked, run /tasks while a subagent is running. It shows the model on each row.
To force every subagent onto one model, the docs add CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE set to "1".
Skip it if you want some subagents, like a code reviewer, on Sonnet. Forcing overrides the model field in your subagent files.
Layer 2: One git worktree per task
A YOLO run should be disposable. If it goes sideways, I want to delete a folder, not untangle my main branch.
A git worktree is a second checkout of the same repo on its own branch, in its own directory:
When the task is done, merge the branch or throw it away:
Claude Code also has this built in:

That creates the worktree under .claude/worktrees/fix-login at your repo root, on a new branch named worktree-fix-login. Run it again with a different name in another terminal and two agents work in parallel without stepping on each other's edits.

Worktrees protect your code. They do not protect your machine. The agent in that folder can still cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519, and as the story above shows, "an isolated copy" on the same filesystem is not isolation. Which brings me to the layer that matters most.
Layer 3: Isolation. Run the agent where it can't reach your real machine
The DIY route is a container. It is a real step up, and a lot of people start there. Two limits worth knowing:
Containers share the host kernel by default. For an agent running shell commands it wrote itself, a separate kernel is a harder wall.
A container gives you walls, not judgment. It does not know that rm -r is different from npm test. And it is easy to mount a little more of your home folder "just this once."

What I use for this layer is Jozu Agent Guard, specifically Agent Enclave: the part of Agent Guard that runs each agent in its own microVM. Agent Guard is the broader runtime and policy system. Agent Enclave is the isolation runtime.
What it does, in plain terms:
One microVM per agent, with its own Linux kernel. The agent sees the workspace you mount and nothing else from your laptop.
Home directory, SSH keys, Keychain and cloud credentials stay out by default. You pass a credential in explicitly (--pass-env, --pass-cloud-creds) or it isn't there.

The policy engine runs inside the microVM, next to the agent. Every tool call is checked before it runs. Enforcement is local, so it does not depend on a central control plane or an internet connection. After you pull policies once, it works offline.
Fails closed. An evaluation error blocks the call instead of skipping the check.

Tamper-evident audit log. Every decision is written to a log on the host, outside the microVM, where the agent can't reach it. Each record carries a hash of the previous one, so edits are detectable on review. That does not make the file uneditable: a user with shell access on the host can still modify it. The chain is what makes any change visible.
Supported agents today: Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenClaw and Antigravity CLI (Google's successor to Gemini CLI). Custom agents run as container-image runtimes.
Where it runs, plainly: on laptops, it is macOS on Apple Silicon (M1 or later) today. Linux and Windows hosts are on the roadmap. For teams, Agent Enclave also runs on Linux Kubernetes nodes.
Install on a Mac, from the Jozu quickstart:
The Standard tier blocks force push and credential reads, allowlists network domains, and asks for confirmation on destructive commands like rm -rf. No Docker needed.
Policies
Policies are short YAML files with CEL assertions. The assert describes the safe case. When it returns false, the policy's action fires. There are four actions:
Enforce blocks the call
Elicit stops and asks a human to approve
Audit allows it and writes a record
Redact masks sensitive content in prompts and completions (guardrail policies only)
This one is from Jozu's policy schema docs. It blocks force pushes:
The first line of the assert matters. Not every tool call has a command argument, and an unguarded rule fails closed and blocks everything.
Recursive deletes are a better fit for Elicit than Enforce, because sometimes you do want them:

One honest note: on Codex, Agent Guard translates policies into Codex's own rule file, and regex rules like this one don't carry over. The docs suggest adding a plain contains() version alongside for Codex.
Jozu's tagline is the whole point of this article: Turn off the permission prompts. Keep the walls.
The team behind it also built KitOps, a CNCF project, so the OCI and signing side is not an afterthought.
Layer 4: Network. Allowlist, not open internet
A leaked token is only a problem if it can reach somewhere. The network is how secrets leave.
So the agent gets a short list of hosts, not the internet:
github.com
your package registry
your model API
the docs sites you actually use

Inside Agent Enclave, the microVM is its own network boundary, and the Standard policy tier allowlists domains. The Strict tier goes further, with localhost-only networking and no ssh, scp or rsync. There is also a kill switch that instantly blocks all network egress. If a run starts doing something I don't recognize, I cut the network first and read the log second.
Not on a Mac, or not ready for a VM yet? Claude Code's built-in sandbox gives you a domain allowlist for shell commands:
Pair it with deny rules for files you never want read:

Two caveats from the docs. The sandbox covers Bash and the processes it starts, not the built-in WebFetch and WebSearch tools, which follow permission rules instead. And it runs on your real machine, not behind a separate kernel. It is a good floor. It is not the same as a wall.
Layer 5: Review the diff, not the chat
The agent's summary of what it did is a story. The diff is what actually happened.
At the end of every run:
The rules:
Small PRs. One task, one worktree, one PR. If the diff is too big to read, the task was too big.
Tests run before merge, not "the agent said tests pass."
Read every changed config file. CI files, lockfiles, .claude/settings.json, anything that changes what runs next time.
Check the audit log for anything that was blocked or needed approval. agentguard logs tails it.
A read-only review subagent that runs git diff and flags issues is worth having. It does not replace reading the diff yourself.
My YOLO checklist
Boring. Saves you a very bad day.
Claude Code, Codex and Cursor ship something new almost every week, and this setup changes with them. Follow me (@Arindam_1729) and I'll post the updated version every time one of them does.
If you want to try the isolation layer: https://jozu.com/agent-guard/

data.markdown:
```yaml
apiVersion: gerty.jozu.dev/v1
kind: ToolPolicy
metadata:
name: confirm-recursive-delete
spec:
match:
tool:
names:
- "Bash"
action: Elicit
elicitation:
message: "This command deletes files recursively. Check the exact path before approving."
rules:
- name: confirm-recursive-delete
assert: |
!("command" in tool.arguments) ||
!tool.arguments.command.matches("(?i)(^|[;&|] *)rm +(-[a-z]* +)*-[a-z]*[rR]")
message: "Recursive delete (rm -r) requires operator confirmation"

```

```markdown
BEFORE I TURN ON AUTO-APPROVE

[ ] Opus plans, Sonnet codes, Haiku runs subagents
[ ] New git worktree for this task
[ ] Agent runs in its own microVM (Agent Enclave)
[ ] No home folder, SSH keys, browser sessions or cloud creds inside
[ ] Policy: block force push, ask before rm -r, audit the rest
[ ] Network allowlist, not open internet
[ ] Kill switch within reach
[ ] Read the diff, run the tests, small PR
[ ] Delete the worktree when done
```

```bash
git worktree add -b fix-login ../myapp-fix-login
cd ../myapp-fix-login
claude --dangerously-skip-permissions
```

```yaml
apiVersion: gerty.jozu.dev/v1
kind: ToolPolicy
metadata:
  name: no-force-push
spec:
  match:
    tool:
      names:
        - "Bash"
  action: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: no-force-push
      assert: |
        !("command" in tool.arguments) ||
        (!tool.arguments.command.contains("git push --force") &&
         !tool.arguments.command.contains("git push -f"))
      message: "Force push is prohibited by security policy"
```

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jozu-ai/agent-guard/main/scripts/install.sh | bash
agentguard --version
agentguard policy add jozu.ml/jozu/agentguard-policies:vm-standard
agentguard run claude-code --workspace ~/projects/myapp
```

```bash
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../myapp-fix-login
git branch -D fix-login # only if you are discarding the work
```
